title: Prove byte-address alignment separately from vectorized element indices
applies_when: A compiler widens global memory accesses based on loop indices while buffer base pointers, declared alignment or matched views may have weaker runtime alignment than the instruction width requires; or a JIT specialization rejects a supported packed-cache block stride.
lesson: An element index divisible by the lane count does not prove that the final byte address is aligned to the access size. Check base-pointer alignment, view offsets, per-row and per-block strides separately, then inspect the generated instruction/helper. Reproduce with an explicitly supported alignment contract and independent source/destination offsets; an arbitrary misaligned call that violates the API contract is not a bug. When stronger alignment is not proven, an address-checked wide fast path can reuse a narrower aligned fallback. Conversely, a specialization can demand more alignment than its unchanged instructions need: vLLM's V4.1 MXFP8 record is 528 bytes, so odd row padding produces a block stride aligned to 16 but not 32 bytes despite a 32-byte-aligned base. Its 128-bit copies work after relaxing only the stride specialization to 16; do not also weaken the base assumption or modify producer padding without evidence. Compare aligned and odd-padding inputs through the writer and real decode/gather consumers, preserving numerical assertions. Validate enabled/disabled predicates, untouched destination sentinels and architecture/toolkit branches; retain a native aligned control alongside the fault or incorrect result.
avoid_when: A compiler or API may already prove or require the stronger alignment; do not impose runtime checks or relax declared strides universally. The TileLang fix covers 16-byte versus 32-byte alignment, not arbitrary byte alignment. Native SM120 correctness and SM89 PTX compilation do not establish B200 execution, full compiler correctness or the performance cost of the extra branch. The separate vLLM B300 result uses source overlays on an existing native runtime, six selected V4.1 tests, two separate legacy controls and a reduced dummy eager MRV2 engine; not official-weight accuracy, production graphs, full-main builds or speedup. Its submitted PR is not merged evidence or a measured Scout-conversion gain. Expected device faults belong in bounded owned processes; do not repeat a poisoned-context experiment on shared devices merely to increase test counts.

evidence.note: Submitted kernel source retains assumed_align32 while reducing only stride divisibility32->16; existing cp.async data copies are128bit. An immutable source mechanism, not all-layout or performance proof.

Reports identical six-case B300 comparison: baseline four pass/two odd-padding FP8 failures, changed kernel six pass; existing V4 reference controls separately two pass. Reduced actual MRV2 startup fails before the change and generates two tokens after. Full CI and official weights/graphs were not qualified; DCO/line review and publication are distinct from maintainer acceptance.
PTX specifies natural alignment to the total access size and undefined behavior for misaligned accesses. This documents the instruction contract, not the reachability of a particular compiler path.

The source investigation distinguishes element-index planning from runtime buffer addresses and corrects the earlier claim that public vectorized loops bypass legalization. Its matched-view route remains source evidence rather than an independent GPU result.

Reports an aligned native control, a 16-modulo-32 misaligned-address failure, identical generated source for explicit align=16, two fresh four-case candidate regressions, and 32 predicate/L2 helper controls on RTX 5090. Testing uses the existing compiler with the exact changed header; no full-current-main build, B200 or performance claim.
